You say one sentence, and six layers relay it behind the scenes.

ⓘ Notes
You say one sentence, and six layers relay it behind the scenes: the agent program orchestrates and acts, the LLM does the “thinking” and “writing”, training builds the skills offline, and compute makes it all run.

Why it’s designed this way: Each layer does one job: the model can be swapped, tools added, training redone, without affecting each other.

🧒 In plain words first

When you say one sentence to an AI, six layers pass the job along behind it, like a restaurant where someone orders, someone plans, someone cooks and someone buys the food.

  • You: say what you want.
  • Agent app: the helper that plans what to do first and next, and goes off to look things up or press buttons for you.
  • Large model: the brain that does the “thinking” and “writing”.
  • Multimodal: eyes, ears and a paintbrush, so it can see pictures, hear sounds and draw.
  • Training: school; the brain learned its skills in advance.
  • Compute: the power station and the kitchen that make it all actually run.

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

Remember each layer in one sentence:

  • Your sentence: where everything starts.
  • Agent app: a helper that can actually do things.
  • Large model: reads some text, then writes what comes next, one small piece at a time.
  • Multimodal: turns pictures and sounds into pieces the model can read, or back again.
  • Training: first reads a huge amount of text to learn the basics, then learns the rules.
  • Compute: thousands of graphics chips (GPUs) working together.

Those “small pieces” are called tokens: the smallest units the model reads and writes, roughly a short word or part of a word.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

To be more exact…A token is not always exactly one word: it can be a whole word, part of a word, or a punctuation mark. Each model’s tokenizer decides how text is cut up.

The user’s sentence

Where the whole system starts: saying what you want in plain words.

Real products are not always layered this neatly: some build retrieval into the model service, others make multimodality a “native” all-in-one model. This diagram is a generic skeleton to aid understanding.
③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

Why split it into layers? Like a school with teachers, cooks and drivers, each does what it is best at: the large model is good at “thinking” (understanding you, deciding the next step), and ordinary programs are good at “doing” (following instructions exactly, connecting to other systems, checking permissions).

Because they are separate, you can swap in a better model, add a new tool or retrain, without rebuilding the other layers.

There is a cost: the more steps, the more chances that one step goes wrong, and the longer it takes.

Go deeper (the full explanation)
Agent app layerWraps the LLM into a program that “gets things done”: planning, tool calls, memory, loops, permissions.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Separate “thinking” (the model) from “doing” (the program): the model is good at understanding and deciding, the program at precise execution, connecting systems and checking permissions. Each does what it’s good at.

✅ Why this works

The model’s weaknesses (no up-to-date information, imprecise arithmetic, no access to external systems) are covered by tools; results come back before the model, and mistakes can be corrected, so it is far more reliable than a “one-shot answer”.

⚠️ Limits / notes: With more steps errors accumulate; cost and waiting time grow with the number of loops; implementations differ a lot between products.

LLM (large language model)The agent’s “brain”: reads a passage of text and writes what comes next, one token at a time.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Every task is unified as “continuing text”: answering, translating, coding and outputting tool-call JSON are all continuation. One format, one model, covering a vast range of tasks.

✅ Why this works

Huge amounts of text force the model to compress grammar, common sense and patterns of reasoning into its parameters; later training teaches it to write according to instructions, in the right format and politely. Empirically, the bigger the scale and the better the data, the more capable it is.

⚠️ Limits / notes: It “hallucinates” (sounds right but is wrong); its knowledge has a cutoff date; it can still make mistakes in precise calculation and long chains of reasoning.

Multimodal encoders / decodersThe LLM’s “eyes, ears and paintbrush”: turning images and sounds into tokens, or tokens back into images and sounds.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Neural networks only understand numbers. As long as every modality becomes the same kind of “vector sequence”, the same powerful architecture (especially the Transformer) can handle them all, instead of building a separate machine for each kind of data.

✅ Why this works

Methods like contrastive learning use huge numbers of “image–text” and “audio–text” pairs to pull different modalities into the same “meaning space”, which is why a model can “describe a picture” or generate an image from text.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Cutting and compressing lose detail (small text, counts and exact positions often go wrong); architectures differ a lot between companies — only the common ideas are covered here.

Training systemWhere the model’s skills come from: pretraining → instruction tuning → preference alignment → reasoning RL.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

“Learning everything” is split into a relay: first lay the foundation with the cheapest, most plentiful data, then teach the rules with small amounts of high-quality data, and finally fine-tune behaviour with rewards. Each leg solves just one problem.

✅ Why this works

Self-supervision means data scale is barely limited by human labelling; fine-tuning and alignment need relatively little data to “steer” general abilities in a useful direction — because the abilities are mostly already there after pretraining.

⚠️ Limits / notes: The exact process differs between teams and changes fast; why each stage works is largely an empirical conclusion; training is extremely expensive.

Compute and servingMakes the model actually run: GPU clusters, inference serving, KV cache, batching, quantization.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

For every token it generates, an LLM has to “run through” billions of parameters, which is very demanding on memory bandwidth. The core engineering question: how to make one GPU serve more people at once, and each token cheaper.

✅ Why this works

Batching lets one read of the weights serve many requests; the KV cache turns each step from “recompute the whole sentence” into “compute only the new token”; quantization makes the weights smaller and faster to read. Combined, they can cut costs a lot (the exact multiple varies by system).

⚠️ Limits / notes: Optimizations often trade off against each other (speed vs quality vs memory); the numbers are empirical and change quickly with hardware and software.

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

Using AI comes with rules, like checking the traffic lights before crossing the road:

  • Copyright: books, drawings and photos made by others are protected by law; whether AI may learn from them, and who owns what AI makes, is still being discussed in each country.
  • Privacy: using someone’s personal details, such as their name, photo or phone number, generally needs their consent first (unless the law says otherwise).
  • Label it: pictures, videos and text made by AI should say “made by AI” when you share them.

This is only an overview, not legal advice; always check the latest official rules.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

Compliance: copyright, privacy, AI-content labelling: an overview, not legal advice; check the latest official texts.

  • China’s main rules: the Interim Measures for Generative AI Services took effect on 15 August 2023 and cover generative AI services offered to the public in China; training data and base models must be lawfully sourced and not infringe IP, and personal information needs consent or another legal basis.
  • Content labels: the Measures for Labelling AI-Generated Content took effect on 1 September 2025. Explicit labels are text, sound or graphic notices users can clearly perceive; implicit labels sit in file metadata and include the content attribute, the provider’s name or code, and a content ID. Users publishing generated content should declare it and use the platform’s labelling feature.
  • Personal information: the Personal Information Protection Law (in force since 1 November 2021) requires a clear purpose and minimum necessary collection; sensitive information (such as biometrics, health, financial accounts, whereabouts) needs separate consent; for automated decisions with a major effect on a person, they can ask for an explanation.
  • EU: Article 50 of the AI Act requires telling people they are interacting with an AI system, marking generated audio, image, video and text in a machine-readable way, and disclosing deep fakes; under Article 113 it applies from 2 August 2026.
  • Copyright: whether AI output can be copyrighted, and whether training on works is permissible, is still debated. The U.S. Copyright Office has published a report in parts (digital replicas, copyrightability, training).
